content: The recommended loading dose of itraconazole is based on pharmacokinetic data. Treatment should continue for a minimum of three months and until the active fungal infection has resolved. Insufficient treatment duration may result in recurrence of the infection. Itraconazole is indicated for the treatment of blastomycosis, including pulmonary and extrapulmonary infections, in both immunocompromised and non-immunocompromised adults. It is also indicated for pulmonary and extrapulmonary aspergillosis in adults who are intolerant of or refractory to amphotericin B therapy. Additionally, itraconazole is used to treat histoplasmosis, including chronic cavitary pulmonary disease and disseminated non-meningeal histoplasmosis, in both immunocompromised and non-immunocompromised adults. It is also indicated for the treatment of onychomycosis of the toenail caused by Trichophyton rubrum. Itraconazole capsules and oral solution are not interchangeable, as only the oral solution has been proven effective for oral and/or esophageal candidiasis. The safety and efficacy of itraconazole have not been established in certain populations. Itraconazole increases the levels of several drugs by inhibiting the metabolism mediated by the hepatic/intestinal enzyme CYP3A4, leading to potential drug interactions and contraindications. Drug Interactions and Contraindications: 1. Alfuzosin: Itraconazole increases alfuzosin levels and prolongs the QTc interval. Co-administration is contraindicated. 2. Avanafil: Itraconazole increases avanafil levels via CYP3A4 inhibition. Co-administration is contraindicated. 3. Conivaptan: Co-administration with itraconazole is contraindicated during and for two weeks after itraconazole treatment due to increased drug levels. 4. Dihydroergotamine (oral and intranasal): Itraconazole increases dihydroergotamine levels, raising the risk of ergotism, cerebral ischemia, and extremity ischemia. Co-administration is contraindicated. 5. Disopyramide: Both drugs prolong the QTc interval, and itraconazole increases disopyramide levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 6. Dofetilide: Itraconazole increases dofetilide levels and prolongs the QTc interval. Co-administration is contraindicated. 7. Dronedarone: Both drugs prolong the QTc interval, and itraconazole increases dronedarone levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 8. Eliglustat: Co-administration is contraindicated in poor or intermediate metabolizers of CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 inhibitors due to increased eliglustat levels. 9. Eplerenone: Itraconazole increases eplerenone levels, raising the risk of hyperkalemia and hypotension. Co-administration is contraindicated. 10. Ergotamine: Itraconazole increases ergotamine levels, leading to a higher risk of ergotism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 11. Felodipine: Itraconazole increases felodipine levels, and both drugs have additive negative inotropic effects. Co-administration is contraindicated. 12. Fesoterodine: Co-administration is contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment due to increased fesoterodine levels and risk of fatal adverse events. 13. Finerinone: Itraconazole increases finerinone levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 14. Flibanserin: Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of severe hypotension or syncope. 15. Geprione: Itraconazole increases geprione levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 16. Indapamide: Both drugs prolong the QTc interval. Co-administration is contraindicated. 17. Irinotecan (including liposomal formulations): Itraconazole increases irinotecan levels, leading to elevated SN-38 metabolite concentrations. Co-administration is contraindicated during and for two weeks after itraconazole treatment. 18. Isavuconazonium sulfate: Itraconazole increases isavuconazonium levels. Co-administration is contraindicated. 19. Ivabradine: Co-administration is contraindicated during and for two weeks after itraconazole treatment due to increased ivabradine levels. 20. Lomitapide: Co-administration is contraindicated during and for two weeks after itraconazole treatment due to increased lomitapide levels. 21. Lonafarnib: Co-administration is contraindicated due to increased lonafarnib levels. 22. Lovastatin: Co-administration is contraindicated during and for two weeks after itraconazole treatment due to increased lovastatin levels and risk of rhabdomyolysis. 23. Lurasidone: Co-administration is contraindicated due to increased lurasidone levels. 24. Mavacamten: 25. Methadone: Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. 26. Methylergonovine: Co-administration is contraindicated due to the risk of ergotism. 27. Midazolam (oral): Co-administration is contraindicated during and for two weeks after itraconazole treatment. IV midazolam should be used cautiously with dose adjustments. 28. Naloxegol: Co-administration is contraindicated due to increased naloxegol levels, which may precipitate opioid withdrawal symptoms. 29. Nisoldipine: Co-administration is contraindicated due to additive negative inotropic effects. 30. Pacritinib: Co-administration is contraindicated due to increased pacritinib levels. 31. Pimozide: Co-administration is contraindicated due to QT prolongation. 32. Quinidine: Co-administration is contraindicated due to QT prolongation. 33. Ranolazine: Co-administration is contraindicated due to increased cardiovascular risks, including QT prolongation. 34. Silodosin: Co-administration is contraindicated due to increased silodosin levels. 35. Simvastatin: Co-administration is contraindicated during and for two weeks after itraconazole treatment due to increased risk of rhabdomyolysis. 36. Solifenacin: Co-administration is contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment due to increased solifenacin levels. 37. Ticagrelor: Co-administration is contraindicated during and for two weeks after itraconazole treatment. 38. Tolvaptan: 39. Triazolam: Co-administration is contraindicated due to QT prolongation. 40. Ubrogepant: Co-administration is contraindicated due to increased ubrogepant levels. 41. Venetoclax: Co-administration is contraindicated during the initial ramp-up phase. Dose adjustments are required after this phase. 42. Voclosporin: Co-administration is contraindicated due to QT prolongation. 43. Acalabrutinib: Avoid co-administration. If unavoidable, temporarily interrupt acalabrutinib treatment. 44. Adagrasib: Avoid co-administration until steady-state concentrations are achieved. 45. Ado-trastuzumab emtansine: Avoid co-administration. If unavoidable, monitor for adverse reactions. 46. Afatinib: Dose reduction is recommended if co-administration is necessary. 47. Aliskiren: Avoid co-administration. If unavoidable, monitor for respiratory depression and sedation. 48. Almotriptan: Avoid co-administration in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 49. Alprazolam: Avoid co-administration due to increased alprazolam levels. 50. Amiodarone: Avoid co-administration due to additive QT prolongation effects. 51. Amisulpride: ECG monitoring is recommended if co-administration is necessary. 52. Anagrelide: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 53. Apalutamide: Avoid co-administration two weeks before and during itraconazole treatment. 54. Aprepitant: Avoid co-administration due to increased aprepitant levels. 55. Aripiprazole: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 56. Artemether: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 57. Artemether/lumefantrine: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 58. Asenapine: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 59. Atorvastatin: Limit atorvastatin dose to 20 mg/day if co-administration is necessary. 60. Avapritinib: Avoid co-administration due to increased avapritinib levels. 61. Axitinib: Dose reduction is recommended if co-administration is unavoidable. 62. Bazedoxifene/conjugated estrogens: Avoid co-administration due to increased drug levels. 63. Bedaquiline: Avoid co-administration for more than 14 consecutive days unless benefits outweigh risks. 64. Bosutinib: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 65. Brigatinib: Dose reduction is recommended if co-administration is unavoidable. 66. Bromocriptine: Avoid co-administration due to increased bromocriptine levels. 67. Budesonide: Monitor for corticosteroid excess if co-administration is necessary. 68. Buprenorphine: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 69. Cabazitaxel: Dose reduction is recommended if co-administration is unavoidable. 70. Cabozantinib: Dose reduction is recommended if co-administration is unavoidable. 71. Calcitriol: Avoid co-administration due to increased calcitriol levels. 72. Capivasertib: Dose reduction is recommended if co-administration is unavoidable. 73. Carbamazepine: Avoid co-administration two weeks before, during, and after itraconazole treatment. 74. Ceritinib: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 75. Chloroquine: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 76. Citalopram: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 77. Clarithromycin: Avoid co-administration due to increased clarithromycin levels. 78. Clozapine: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 79. Cobicistat: Avoid co-administration due to increased cobicistat levels. 80. Cobimetinib: Avoid co-administration due to increased cobimetinib levels. 81. Colchicine: Avoid co-administration in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 82. Conjugated estrogens: Avoid co-administration due to increased drug levels. 83. Copanlisib: Dose reduction is recommended if co-administration is unavoidable. 84. Crizotinib: Dose reduction is recommended if co-administration is unavoidable. 85. Dabrafenib: Avoid co-administration due to QT prolongation. 86. Daridorexant: Avoid co-administration due to increased daridorexant levels. 87. Darifenacin: Avoid co-administration due to increased darifenacin levels.
